cues.text: Imagine you own a small order service.

The team says it wants AI to speed up
coding,

so you pull up the last few routine
fixes.

One was ready on Tuesday and received
its first useful review on Thursday.

Across the baseline, the wait was
eighteen business hours.

That gives us a better starting
question.

Could a small, well-tested change be
easier for a teammate to pick up?

Mark that waiting step, then choose a
task with a result the reviewer can

verify, like fixing the minimum order
quantity.

Here is the task a developer could hand
to a coding assistant.

The order validator accepts zero, and
the minimum is one.
Put four examples in the ticket.
One and five pass.
Zero and negative one are rejected.

Verify the two existing behaviors as
well as the new one.

Write the zero test first, run it while
the old comparison is still in place,
and save the failure.
After the fix, run all four cases again.

A reviewer can now trace the request to
test evidence in the pull request.

Open the validator and its tests in
Visual Studio Code.

The author can ask Copilot for a plan
here,

then inspect the changes in the same
editor.

Claude Code and OpenCode run in the
approved corporate Google Cloud
workspace.

Those remain options when a task
benefits from tools that are already
available there.

This exercise needs a two-file change
and a standard test command,
so use the editor workflow.

Record the tool you selected and where
its actions run before discussing model
choices.

Suppose your organization has enabled
two models for this editor.
Call them A and B.

Prepare eight synthetic cases with known
expected behavior.

Give each model a fresh copy of the same
starting point and the same time limit
for each case.

A reviewer marks a pass only when the
tests, scope,
and evidence all meet the ticket.

For instance, a working change without
its zero regression test still misses
the evidence requirement.

In a second column, log the minutes the
author spent steering the assistant or
repairing its output.

In this exercise, A passes seven of
eight.
B passes eight of eight.

The median steering time is two minutes
for A and three for B.

We agreed up front that every case had
to pass, including the regression check.

B clears the gate for one extra median
minute of author effort.

Choose B for the pilot and keep that
trade-off visible.

If you chose based on speed alone, you
would pick A, so test yourself now.

Which criterion rules out A, and where
would the reviewer see the missing
evidence?

Save a short note with the task, the
tool and model choice,

the dated benchmark with its sample
size, and the pilot owner.

In our example, the engineering lead
starts with routine validator fixes in
Visual Studio Code.

Model B is the better option in these
eight synthetic cases.

If the organization changes the
available model,

if the pilot starts touching other parts
of the order service,

or if review quality slips, bring the
choice back for review.

Now fill in those four fields for a task
your team already handles.
